screen:
At Harrowgate, the walled road town of the Marches, petitioners used to knock on the king's shield. {name} set it beside the judgement chair so a voice too small to carry through the hall could reach him through the iron. He had inherited the crown young. He learned the weight of grain, the price of a repaired axle, and how neatly a clerk could write a decision that somebody outside would have to survive.

Harrowgate stood between the Tanglewood and the raider hills. Its roads brought carts, banner companies and families travelling with everything they owned. {name} wanted a city that could endure another winter. He paid for stone, ordered grain stored, and required the gates to close at the evening bell. At first, the rule seemed wise. The granaries filled. The walls held. People praised a king who could make a difficult choice.

Then a cart overturned outside the gate after the bell. An injured carter lay under its axle; his daughter knocked on the iron and asked for hands to lift it. The watch would not open without the king's seal. {name} heard the knocking from his hall and sent the seal ahead of him. By the time he reached the road, the cart was upright and the carter was dead. The daughter returned the seal. She kept her father's coat.

{name} carried the man inside himself. He laid the crown beside the body and spent the night trying to warm hands that could no longer close. He had sworn over that crown to keep the people of his city safe. Before morning, violet fire appeared in the shield's seams. When he lifted it, the man remained dead, but a wounded watchman beside the table stopped bleeding. The fire had answered the promise. It had not forgiven the decision.

He has ruled from an open hall since then. The shield stands beside his chair; the mace lies within reach, and violet fire burns across the black plate he wears to hear petitions. He sends guards to meet late carts instead of leaving travellers outside a locked gate. It costs grain and sleep, and the raids have not ended. News of Joss Gatley holding Harrowmere's east gate reached him with the other border reports. {name} ordered the wounded received without waiting for a second seal.

He still keeps the first seal. Recently a carter brought him a coat clasp and a message from the woman who had once knocked outside his gate. She was bringing injured people down from the raider hills and needed safe passage. {name} has ordered the road watched for her cart. Each evening he goes out before the bell, carrying the shield. This time, she will find him on the road.
narration:
At Harrowgate, people used to knock on my shield when they wanted judgement.
It stood beside my chair in the hall, where even a child could reach the iron.
You could hear a small knock through a room full of men arguing over grain.
I liked that. I thought it made me a good king.
My father left me the crown before I knew what a broken axle cost.
So I learned. Grain by the sack, stone by the cart, names by the household.
Our town stood between the Tanglewood and the raider hills.
Every road brought somebody asking whether the walls had room for them.
I wanted those walls to last. I wanted a winter nobody had to fear.
We filled the stores, repaired the stone, and closed the gates at the evening bell.
The rule was mine. My seal was the only thing that could open them afterward.
People thanked me for being firm. I began to enjoy being thanked.
Then a cart overturned on the road outside, just after the bell.
A carter lay beneath the axle. His daughter came to the gate for help.
She knocked on the iron. The watch sent for my seal.
I heard her from the hall, and sent it ahead while I put my coat on.
When I reached the road, they had lifted the cart.
Her father was dead. She put my seal into my hand.
Then she took his coat, because the night was cold, and walked away.
I carried him inside. He was heavier than I expected.
I laid my crown on the table beside him and tried to warm his hands.
I had sworn over that crown to keep our people safe.
I said the promise again. And again, until there was no voice left in me.
Before morning, violet fire shone through the seams of my shield.
I lifted it. A watchman beside the table had cut his arm on the axle.
His bleeding stopped. The man on the table did not move.
That is how the fire came to me. I have never called it forgiveness.
I wear the black plate in the judgement hall now, with the shield beside my chair.
The mace stays near my hand. A crown does not stop the raids.
But the hall stays open, and guards go out to meet the late carts.
It costs us grain. It costs the watch their sleep. I hear every complaint.
When word came that Joss Gatley had held Harrowmere's east gate, I sent one order back.
Receive the wounded. Do not wait for another seal.
Last week a carter brought me a coat clasp. I knew it before he spoke.
The girl who left her father with me is a woman now, bringing injured people down from the hills.
She asked for safe passage. Nothing else. She owes me nothing else.
I have the road watched for her cart, and I go out before the bell.
If you need judgement tonight, you will have to knock on my shield out there.
